method: The vertical drop is the water depth plus the height of the bow roller above the waterline, both in metres. The rode to deploy is the scope multiplied by that drop, where the scope is the rode length divided by the drop, so 5 means 5:1. With the rode straight and taut the bow sits a horizontal distance √(rode² − drop²) from the anchor, which is the swing circle radius, and twice that is the diameter; the rode's angle below horizontal at the bow is asin(drop/rode). The extra rode each extra metre of depth needs is the scope itself, which is what a falling or rising tide adds. A slack chain hangs in a catenary and reaches less than the taut figure, so the radius is the room the boat can use rather than a guaranteed position. Values are refused outside 0.5 to 100 m of depth, 0 to 10 m of bow roller height and a scope of 1.5 to 20, and decimal commas are accepted. The page does not model holding ground, weather, anchor type, chain size, snubbing or local rules, it makes no claim about whether an anchorage is safe, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Anchoring scope is quoted as the ratio of rode length to the vertical distance from the bow roller to the seabed, so the rode is the scope times the water depth plus the bow height.
A straight taut rode of length L dropping a vertical distance H puts the bow √(L² − H²) horizontally from the anchor, which bounds the circle the boat swings through.
A hanging chain forms a catenary rather than a straight line, so the horizontal reach at a given scope is smaller than the taut-ride geometry suggests.
